2 Preliminaries

Given a number k∈ℕ>1k\in\mathbb{N}_{>1} and an undirected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with
non-negative edge weights, ω:E→ℝ>0\omega:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0},
the graph partitioning problem (GPP) asks for a partition Π\Pi of VV with
blocks of nodes Π=(V1CLOSE\Pi=(V_{1},…,OPENVk)V_{k}):

1.\displaystyle 1.\,\,\,\,
V1∪⋯∪Vk=V\displaystyle V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k}=V

2.\displaystyle 2.\,\,\,\,
Vi∩Vj=∅​∀i≠j.\displaystyle V_{i}\cap V_{j}=\emptyset\,\,\,\forall i\neq j.

A balance constraint demands that all blocks have about equal weights. More precisely, it requires
that, ∀i∈{1,…,k}:|Vi|≤Lmax:= (1+ϵ)⌈|V|/k⌉\forall i\in\{1,\dots,k\}:|V_{i}|\leq L_{\max}\mbox{\rm:= }(1+\epsilon)\lceil|V|/k\rceil for
some imbalance parameter ϵ∈ℝ≥0\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.
In the case of ϵ=0\epsilon=0, one also uses the term perfectly balanced.
Sometimes we also use weighted nodes with node weights c:V→ℝ>0c:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}.
Weight functions on nodes and edges are extended to sets of such objects by summing their weights.
A block ViV_{i} is overloaded if |Vi|>Lmax|V_{i}|>L_{\max}.
A clustering is also a partition of the nodes. However, kk is usually not given in advance, and the balance constraint is removed.
Note that a partition is also a clustering of a graph.
In both cases, the goal is to minimize or maximize a particular objective function.
We recall well-known objective functions for GPP in Section 2.1.
A node vv is a neighbor of node uu if there is an edge {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E.
If a node v∈Viv\in V_{i} has a neighbor w∈Vjw\in V_{j}, i≠ji\neq j, then it is called boundary node.
An edge that runs between blocks is also called cut edge.
The set Ei​j:= {{u,v}∈E:u∈Vi,v∈Vj}E_{ij}\mbox{\rm:= }\left\{\left\{u,v\right\}\in E:u\in V_{i},v\in V_{j}\right\} is the set of cut edges between two blocks ViV_{i} and VjV_{j}.
An abstract view of the partitioned graph is the so called quotient graph or communication graph, where nodes represent blocks,
and edges are induced by connectivity between blocks. There is an edge in the quotient graph between blocks ViV_{i} and
VjV_{j} if and only if there is an edge between a node in ViV_{i} and a node in VjV_{j} in the original, partitioned graph.
The degree d⁡(v)d(v) of a node vv is the number of its neighbors.
An adjacency matrix of a graph is a |V|×|V||V|\times|V| matrix describing node connectivity.
The element au,va_{u,v} of the matrix specifies the weight of the edge from node uu to node vv.
It is set to zero if there is no edge between these nodes.
The Laplacian matrix of a graph GG is defined as L=D−AL=D-A, where DD is the diagonal matrix expressing node degrees, and AA is the adjacency matrix.
A cycle in a directed graph with negative weight is also called negative cycle.
A matching M⊆EM\subseteq E is a set of edges that do not share any common nodes, i. e., the graph (V,M)(V,M) has maximum degree one.

2.1 Objective Functions

In practice, one often seeks to find a partition that minimizes (or maximizes) an objective. Probably the most prominent objective function is to minimize the total cut

∑i<jω⁡(Ei​j).\sum_{i<j}\omega(E_{ij}).

(2.1)

Other formulations of GPP exist.
For instance when GP is used in parallel computing
to map the graph nodes to different processors, the
communication volume is often more appropriate than the
cut [HK00].
For a block ViV_{i}, the communication volume is defined as comm(ViV_{i}) := ∑v∈Vic(v)D(v)\mbox{\rm:= }\sum_{v\in V_{i}}c(v)D(v), where D⁡(v)D(v) denotes the number of different blocks in which vv has a neighbor node, excluding ViV_{i}.
The maximum communication volume is then defined as maxi⁡ comm(​Vi\max_{i}\text{ comm(}V_{i}), whereas the total communication volume
is defined as ∑i comm(​Vi\sum_{i}\text{ comm(}V_{i}).
The maximum communication volume was used in one subchallenge of the 10th DIMACS Challenge on Graph Partitioning and Graph Clustering [BMSW13].
Although some applications profit from other objective functions
such as the communication volume or block shape (formalized by the block’s aspect ratio [DPSW00a],
minimizing the cut size has been adopted as a kind of standard.
One reason is that cut optimization seems to be easier in practice.
Another one is that for graphs with high structural locality the cut
often correlates with most other formulations but other objectives make it more difficult to use a multilevel approach.

There are also GP formulations in which balance is not directly encoded in the problem description but integrated into the objective function. For example, the expansion of a non-trivial cut (V1,V2)(V_{1},V_{2}) is defined as ω⁡(E12)/min⁡(c⁡(V1),c⁡(V2))\omega(E_{12})/\min({c(V_{1}),c(V_{2})}).
Similarly, the conductance of such a cut is defined as ω⁡(E12)/min⁡(vol​(V1),vol​(V2))\omega(E_{12})/\min(\text{vol}(V_{1}),\text{vol}(V_{2})), where vol​(S):=∑v∈Sd​(v)\text{vol}(S):=\sum_{v\in S}d(v) denotes the volume of the set SS.

As an extension to the problem, when the application graph changes over time,
repartitioning becomes necessary. Due to changes in the underlying application,
a graph partition may become gradually imbalanced due to the introduction
of new nodes (and edges) and the deletion of others.
Once the imbalance exceeds
a certain threshold, the application should call the repartitioning routine. This routine
is to compute a new partition Π′\Pi^{\prime} from the old one, Π\Pi.
In many applications it is favorable to keep the changes between Π\Pi and Π′\Pi^{\prime}
small. Minimizing these changes simultaneously to optimizing Π′\Pi^{\prime} with respect
to the cut (or a similar objective) leads to multiobjective optimization. To avoid the
complexity of the latter, a linear combination of both objectives seems
feasible in practice [SKK00].

2.2 Hypergraph Partitioning

A hypergraph H=(V,E)H=(V,E) is a generalization of a graph in
which an edge (usually called hyperedge or net) can connect any
number of nodes.
As with graphs, partitioning a hypergraph also means to find an
assignment of nodes to different blocks of (mostly) equal size.
The objective function, however, is usually expressed differently.
A straightforward generalization of the edge cut to hypergraphs is
the hyperedge cut. It counts the number of hyperedges
that connect different blocks. In widespread use for hypergraph
partitioning, however, is the so-called (λ−1)(\lambda-1) metric,
C​V​(H,Π)=∑e∈E(λ⁡(e,Π)−1)CV(H,\Pi)=\sum_{e\in E}(\lambda(e,\Pi)-1),
where λ⁡(e,Π)\lambda(e,\Pi) denotes the number of distinct blocks connected by the
hyperedge ee and Π\Pi the partition of HH’s vertex set.

One drawback of hypergraph partitioning compared to GP is the necessity of
more complex algorithms—in terms of implementation and running time, not necessarily in terms of worst-case
complexity. Paying this price seems only worthwhile if the underlying application profits significantly
from the difference between the graph and the hypergraph model.

To limit the scope, we focus in this paper on GP and forgo a more detailed treatment of hypergraph
partitioning.
Many of the techniques we describe, however, can be or have been transferred to hypergraph partitioning as
well [CA01, PM07, CB+07, TK08, FB13].
One important application area of hypergraph partitioning is VLSI design (see Section 3.5).

2.3 Hardness Results and Approximation

Partitioning a graph into kk blocks of roughly equal size such that the cut metric is minimized is
NP-complete (as decision problem) [HR73, GJS74].
Andreev and Räcke [AR06] have shown that there is no constant-factor approximation
for the perfectly balanced version (ϵ=0\epsilon=0) of this problem on general graphs.
